title: Applet Programming II – Applet Lifecycle & Methods

mcqs.question: What is the first method called in an applet's lifecycle?

options.B: init()

mcqs.explanation: init() is the very first method called when an applet is loaded. It's called exactly once. Used for one-time initialization: creating UI components, setting layout, loading images, setting colors.

mcqs.question: Which method draws text and graphics on the applet surface?

options.B: display()

mcqs.explanation: paint(Graphics g) is called by the system to render the applet's visual content. The Graphics parameter g provides drawing methods: drawString, drawLine, drawRect, drawOval, drawImage, fillRect, etc.

mcqs.question: What does destroy() do in the applet lifecycle?

options.B: Performs final cleanup before the applet is completely unloaded from memory

mcqs.explanation: destroy() is called when the applet is being permanently unloaded (e.g., browser closes, page replaced). Use for final cleanup: closing database connections, stopping threads, releasing resources. After destroy(), the applet object is garbage collected.

mcqs.question: Which method temporarily pauses the applet when the user navigates away?

options.B: stop()

mcqs.explanation: stop() is called when the user leaves the page (minimizes browser, navigates elsewhere). It should pause animations, stop threads, release temporary resources. start() resumes when the user returns.

mcqs.question: How do you draw a line from (10,20) to (100,200) in an applet?
mcqs.explanation: g.drawLine(x1, y1, x2, y2) draws a line from (x1,y1) to (x2,y2). Example: g.drawLine(10, 20, 100, 200) draws a diagonal line. All coordinates are in pixels with (0,0) at top-left.

mcqs.question: Which method draws a filled oval?

options.B: g.fillOval()

mcqs.explanation: g.fillOval(x, y, width, height) draws a filled (solid) oval within the bounding rectangle. g.drawOval() draws only the outline. For a circle, use equal width and height: g.fillOval(x, y, 50, 50).

mcqs.question: What is the role of stop() and start() together?

options.B: They form a pause/resume pair — stop() pauses when leaving page, start() resumes when returning
options.C: stop() starts the applet; start() stops it

mcqs.explanation: stop() is called when navigating away (pause). start() is called when returning (resume). Together they manage the applet's active/inactive state. If stop() stops a timer, start() should restart it. This pair runs multiple times; init() and destroy() run once.

mcqs.question: Which Color constructor creates a custom gray color?
mcqs.explanation: All three work: Color.GRAY (constant), new Color(128,128,128) (RGB constructor), and Color.gray (deprecated lowercase). RGB values range 0-255. new Color(0,0,0) is black; new Color(255,255,255) is white.

mcqs.question: How do you set the font for drawing text in an applet?

options.B: g.font = "Arial Bold 16"

mcqs.explanation: g.setFont(new Font("Arial", Font.BOLD, 16)) sets the font. Parameters: font name ("Arial", "Serif", "Monospaced"), style (Font.PLAIN, Font.BOLD, Font.ITALIC, Font.BOLD|Font.ITALIC), size in points. Subsequent drawString() uses this font.

mcqs.question: What does g.drawString("Hello", 50, 100) do?

options.B: Creates a String variable

mcqs.explanation: g.drawString(text, x, y) draws the text starting at pixel position (x, y). The y coordinate is the baseline of the text (bottom of most characters, not the top). At (50, 100), the text's baseline is at y=100.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between paint() and repaint()?

options.B: paint() is called by the system to draw; repaint() is called by the programmer to request a redraw (which calls update() then paint())
options.D: paint() is called by the programmer; repaint() by the system

mcqs.explanation: paint(Graphics g) is called by the AWT event dispatch thread when the component needs rendering. repaint() is a programmer request — it schedules update() (which clears area and calls paint()). You call repaint(); you never call paint() directly.

mcqs.question: Why is paint() called multiple times during an applet's lifetime?

options.B: The system calls paint() whenever the applet needs redrawing — initial display, window resize, covering/uncovering by another window, or after repaint() request

mcqs.explanation: paint() is called by the system: on first display, when the window is resized, when uncovered after being hidden by another window, and after repaint() requests. This is why paint() should be efficient and always reflect the current state — it may be called at any time.

mcqs.question: What does the update() method do by default, and why is it problematic for animations?

options.B: It clears the entire applet area with background color, then calls paint() — the clearing causes flicker in animations

mcqs.explanation: Default update(Graphics g): fills the component area with the background color, then calls paint(). For animations, this clearing-and-redrawing cycle causes visible flicker. Solution: override update() to call paint() directly (skip clearing) or use double buffering.

mcqs.question: How do you read an applet parameter named 'speed' from the HTML file?

options.B: String s = getParameter("speed"); int speed = Integer.parseInt(s)

mcqs.explanation: getParameter() always returns a String (or null if not defined). Convert as needed: Integer.parseInt(getParameter("speed")). Always check for null: String s = getParameter("speed"); if(s != null) speed = Integer.parseInt(s);

mcqs.question: What is the correct HTML syntax to pass a parameter to an applet?

options.B: <param name="speed" value="10">

mcqs.explanation: Parameters go inside the <applet> tag: <applet code='App.class' width=300 height=300><param name='speed' value='10'></applet>. Multiple parameters: add multiple <param> tags. In Java: getParameter("speed") returns "10".

mcqs.question: How does an applet load and display an image?

options.B: Image img = getImage(getCodeBase(), "image.png"); g.drawImage(img, x, y, this)

mcqs.explanation: getImage(url, filename) loads an image asynchronously from the applet's code base. g.drawImage(img, x, y, this) draws it at (x,y). The 'this' (ImageObserver) handles asynchronous loading notifications. getImage() returns immediately; image may still be loading.

mcqs.question: What happens if you call getParameter() for a parameter not defined in the HTML?

options.B: Returns null

mcqs.explanation: getParameter("undefined") returns null. Always handle null: String val = getParameter("color"); String color = (val != null) ? val : "default"; Failing to check null and calling Integer.parseInt(null) throws NumberFormatException.

mcqs.question: What is getCodeBase() used for?

options.B: Returns the URL of the directory containing the applet's .class files

mcqs.explanation: getCodeBase() returns the URL where the applet's class files reside. If the applet is at http://server.com/applets/App.class, getCodeBase() returns http://server.com/applets/. Used with getImage(getCodeBase(), "logo.png") to load images from the same directory as the applet.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between getCodeBase() and getDocumentBase()?

options.B: getCodeBase() = URL of applet .class directory; getDocumentBase() = URL of the HTML page containing the applet
options.C: getCodeBase() is for images; getDocumentBase() for text

mcqs.explanation: getCodeBase() returns where the applet code lives (e.g., http://server.com/classes/). getDocumentBase() returns where the HTML page is (e.g., http://server.com/pages/index.html). They differ when the HTML page and class files are in different directories.

mcqs.question: How do you override update() to reduce flicker in an animation?

options.A: public void update(Graphics g) { /* do nothing */ }
options.B: public void update(Graphics g) { paint(g); } — skip clearing, just call paint directly
options.C: public void update(Graphics g) { clear(); paint(g); }

mcqs.explanation: Overriding update() to just call paint(g) without clearing the background eliminates the clear-causes-flicker problem. The animation draws over the previous frame. For complete flicker elimination, combine with double buffering: draw to an off-screen image, then copy to screen.

mcqs.question: Why is double buffering more effective than overriding update() for eliminating flicker?

options.B: Overriding update() still draws directly to screen — partial drawings may be visible during the draw. Double buffering draws everything to an off-screen image first, then copies in one operation — the screen never shows intermediate states

mcqs.explanation: update() override: no clearing, but paint() still draws multiple elements directly to screen — if the display refreshes mid-draw, partial content is visible (flicker). Double buffering: paint() draws to an off-screen Image (invisible), then drawImage() copies the complete frame to screen in one fast operation. The screen always shows a complete frame.

mcqs.question: What is the role of ImageObserver in drawImage(), and why is 'this' passed?

options.B: Image loading is asynchronous; ImageObserver receives notifications when image data arrives. 'this' (the applet) implements ImageObserver, so it can repaint when the image is ready

mcqs.explanation: getImage() returns immediately but image data loads asynchronously. drawImage(img, x, y, observer) returns false if the image isn't fully loaded. The ImageObserver (usually 'this' — the applet implements ImageObserver.imageUpdate()) receives callbacks when more image data arrives, triggering repaint() to show progressively loaded images.

mcqs.question: In the applet lifecycle, what is the exact sequence when a user navigates away from a page and then returns?

options.B: stop() is called when leaving; start() is called when returning — init() is NOT called again
options.D: Nothing happens — the applet keeps running

mcqs.explanation: Leaving page: stop() is called (pause). Returning: start() is called (resume). init() is called only once on initial load — NOT repeated. destroy() is called only when the applet is permanently unloaded (browser close). So: init (once) → start → stop → start → stop → ... → destroy (once).

mcqs.question: What is the 'delegation event model' in Java AWT and how does it apply to applets?

options.A: Events are handled by a single loop
options.B: Components generate events; listeners (registered with add*Listener) handle them. In applets, you add listeners in init() and implement handler methods (actionPerformed, etc.)

mcqs.explanation: Delegation Event Model: Event sources (Button, TextField) generate EventObject subclasses (ActionEvent, MouseEvent). Listeners (ActionListener, MouseListener) implement handler interfaces and register with addXXXListener(). When an event occurs, the source calls each registered listener's handler method. In applets: button.addActionListener(this) in init(); actionPerformed(ActionEvent e) handles clicks.

mcqs.question: What thread calls paint() in an applet, and what are the implications for thread safety?

options.B: The AWT Event Dispatch Thread (EDT) — all painting and event handling happens on the EDT; any data paint() reads must be thread-safe or modified only on the EDT
options.C: A new thread per paint call

mcqs.explanation: The AWT Event Dispatch Thread (EDT) is a single thread that handles all painting (paint, repaint) and event handling (actionPerformed, mouseClicked). This means: 1) paint() and event handlers never run concurrently — they're automatically thread-safe with each other, 2) if a background thread modifies data that paint() reads, you must synchronize access to prevent the EDT from seeing inconsistent state.

mcqs.question: What is the security implication of getCodeBase() for applet network connections?

options.B: Applets can only open network connections to getCodeBase() host — preventing applets from connecting to arbitrary servers and exfiltrating data

mcqs.explanation: Applet security: an applet loaded from http://example.com/ can only connect back to example.com, not to other servers. This 'same-origin policy' prevents malicious applets from acting as clients to attack other servers or exfiltrate data. getCodeBase() identifies the trusted origin.

mcqs.question: Why might paint() be called before init() completes, and how should this be handled?

options.B: The system may call paint() before init() finishes if the window becomes visible during initialization. Handle by checking if initialization is done: if(dataReady) { draw } else { draw loading screen }
options.D: This is a bug in Java

mcqs.explanation: The AWT may display the applet window (triggering paint()) while init() is still executing (e.g., init() is loading a large image). paint() may run with partially-initialized state. Defensive pattern: use a boolean 'initialized' flag. In paint(): if(!initialized) { g.drawString("Loading...", 50, 50); return; } else { draw normal content }.

mcqs.question: What is the difference between showStatus() and System.out.println() in an applet?

options.B: showStatus() displays in the browser's status bar (visible to user); System.out.println() goes to the Java console (usually hidden, for debugging only)
options.D: System.out.println() is not available in applets

mcqs.explanation: showStatus(String) displays text in the browser/appletviewer status bar at the bottom — user-visible feedback ('Loading...', 'Ready'). System.out.println() goes to the Java Console (View > Show Console in browser) — developer debugging only, typically not visible to end users. Use showStatus() for user messages, println for debugging.

mcqs.question: How does the applet class hierarchy relate to AWT Component and Container?

options.B: Applet extends Panel which extends Container which extends Component — applets ARE AWT components, inheriting all GUI capabilities

mcqs.explanation: Hierarchy: Object → Component → Container → Panel → Applet. Since Applet extends Panel (which is a Container), applets can: add components (add(button)), set layouts (setLayout), handle events, set background/foreground, and be painted. This makes applets full AWT citizens with all GUI capabilities. JApplet extends Applet and adds Swing support.

mcqs.question: What is the consequence of calling repaint() rapidly in a loop (e.g., in an animation), and how does the coalescing mechanism work?

options.A: Each repaint() immediately repaints — high CPU usage
options.B: repaint() requests are coalesced — multiple rapid calls may result in a single paint() call, as the AWT merges pending repaint requests to avoid excessive painting
options.D: Each repaint() creates a new thread

mcqs.explanation: repaint() posts a paint request to the EDT event queue. If multiple repaint() calls happen before the EDT processes them, the AWT coalesces (merges) them into one paint() call for the union of the dirty regions. This prevents excessive painting and CPU overload. For smooth animation, call repaint() at a controlled rate (e.g., 30-60 FPS via Timer), not in a tight loop.
